title: Tile Compression and Embeddings for Multi-Label Classification in GeoLifeCLEF 2024
venue: CLEF 2024: Conference and Labs of the Evaluation Forum
extended_summary:
This paper is not the requested education study titled “Impact of ChatGPT on the Academic Writing Quality of Senior High School Students” (2024). Instead, it is a technical working note on the GeoLifeCLEF 2024 competition, which focuses on predicting plant species presence/absence at geographic survey sites from remote-sensing, raster, geolocation, and time-series data. The core problem is extreme multi-label classification for biodiversity modeling rather than any instructional or academic-writing intervention.

The authors study several machine-learning approaches for this task: geolocation-only neural models, nearest-neighbor models built with locality-sensitive hashing, CNNs over compressed tile representations using discrete cosine transform (DCT) coefficients, and self-supervised Tile2Vec embeddings for transfer learning. Their pipeline preprocesses large geospatial datasets into tiled and compressed forms to make training more efficient, and they compare multiple loss functions including BCE, ASL, Hill, and sigmoidF1. Performance is evaluated using F1-micro on the competition leaderboard.

The population is not human participants but geospatial survey sites and plant-species labels from Western Europe. The datasets include millions of presence-only and presence-absence examples, along with 128x128 RGB-NIR satellite tiles, raster layers, and quarterly environmental time series over 20 years. The context is a shared-task competition setting rather than a school, classroom, or educational environment.

The main conclusion is that simple geolocation features were surprisingly strong predictors, with the authors’ best public leaderboard score reaching 0.16128, while RGB-IR tile CNNs achieved similar performance and Tile2Vec provided smoother convergence but lower final scores. Overall, their methods underperformed strong competition baselines and top teams, but the paper suggests that compressed spectral representations, spatial nearest-neighbor structure, and self-supervised embeddings remain promising directions for future work in ecological multi-label prediction.
